title: A Mycotoxin-Driven Vagal Mechanism for ALS-Spectrum Motor Neuron Disease: A Hypothesis Supported by Five Years of Case Documentation
content: Background. Approximately 90% of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) cases are sporadic, and the underlying etiology remains incompletely understood [1]. Hypothesis. Chronic colonization of the gastric mucosa by a mycotoxin-producing mold, concealed beneath a mucosal biofilm and therefore potentially undetectable by standard endoscopy, is proposed to drive sustained motor-neuron hyperexcitability through three mechanistically distinct components: (1) TLR activation on vagal afferent fibers projecting excitatory signals to brainstem motor nuclei via neural spill-over; (2) cross-reactive immune attack on motor-neuron surface proteins via molecular mimicry; and (3) Dectin-1-mediated neuroinflammation during biofilm disruption. Case. The index case concerns a male who was 36 years old at symptom onset and whose current clinical diagnosis is Cramp-Fasciculation Syndrome. Although bilateral neurogenic remodeling was documented by electromyography in May 2022, formal diagnostic criteria for ALS were not met because subsequent electrophysiological examinations showed no further progression. Over the following years, motor symptoms fluctuated in close temporal association with multiple interventions and reproducibly returned after their discontinuation. This was accompanied by repeated urinary mycotoxin findings, marked abnormalities in T-cell activation markers and cytokine responses, and multiple internally consistent pharmacological observations. The overall clinical and electrophysiological course subsequently stabilized. A subsequent serum antibody panel showed broad IgG reactivity across all 14 tested mycotoxin analytes and a marked Satratoxin-dominant IgE signal (1.721; exceeding the laboratory’s highest category threshold), whereas a previous mold-specific lymphocyte transformation test was negative for Stachybotrys atra/chartarum and elevated for Candida albicans.
